reference_title: Design and Construction of Continuous Flight Auger Piles

figures.caption: CFA Pile Rig
figures.description: Introduction General description and dimensions of CFA pile systems including ACIP and DD pile types Drilled in one continuous operation with hollow-stem auger; grout/concrete pumped through stem during withdrawal Typical diameter: 300–900 mm (12–36 in.); length up to 30 m (100 ft); min spacing 3–5D Reinforcement placed into fluid grout after auger withdrawal; typically limited to upper 10–15 m No casing or slurry needed; limited to soil or very weak rock (cannot socket into hard rock) Advantages: fast, low noise/vibration, no splices; disadvantages: less reliable QA, soil spoils

figures.caption: Effect of Over-Excavation using CFA Piles
figures.description: Construction Sequence CFA pile installation sequence — drilling, grouting, and reinforcement placement controls Drilling: balance rotation/penetration to keep auger flights full and avoid soil mining (decompression, subsidence) Grouting must begin immediately upon reaching tip depth — delay risks seizing the auger Grout pressure: 1.0–1.7 MPa (150–250 psi) at auger top; must exceed overburden at discharge point Auger lifted 150 mm (6 in.) to blow plug; re-seated at tip; then smoothly withdrawn with no or slow rotation Required grout overrun: 15–20% above theoretical pile volume; continuous monitoring required DD piles: displacement auger densifies surrounding soil, avoids mining in loose sands Rebar: placed into fluid grout immediately after withdrawal; 75 mm min cover; VMAs may be needed

figures.caption: Use of CFA Piles for Commercial Building Projects
figures.description: Advantages and Limitations of CFA Piles Site selection and suitability assessment for CFA piles and drilled displacement piles in transportation projects Favorable soils: medium to very stiff clay, cemented sands, residual soils, medium-dense to dense sands, rock under stiff overburden Unfavorable: very soft soils (necking), loose water-bearing sands (mining), voids/flowing water, hard stratum under soft soil Sand-bearing stratum under stiff clay: slow drilling in clay causes flighting of sand; pile carries only side friction Piles >30 m (100 ft) require unusual high-torque equipment; deep-scour/liquefiable zones require high bending resistance Project favoring conditions: speed-critical, large quantities, low headroom, secant walls ≤10 m, soundwalls, pile-supported embankments

figures.caption: Pilecaps on CFA Piles For A Pile-Supported Embankment
figures.description: Advantages and Limitations of Drilled Displacement Piles Selection and use of drilled displacement piles compared to conventional CFA piles DD piles densify surrounding soil, increase horizontal stress — higher side resistance in granular soils vs. CFA Little or no spoil generated — favorable for contaminated sites or restricted disposal areas Max depth ~20–25 m (65–80 ft) due to high torque demand; cannot be used in rock or hard soils Lateral displacement can affect nearby utilities and structures; large pore pressures possible in loose fine-grained soils

figures.caption: Drilled Displacement Piles Limit Spoil Removal

figures.caption: CFA Pile Foundation for Soundwall
figures.description: Applications for Transportation Projects CFA pile applications for soundwalls, bridge foundations, retaining walls, and pile-supported embankments Soundwalls: single piles 450–900 mm dia., 4–8 m deep, wind-governed lateral load design Bridge foundations: best for interchanges without scour concerns; CFA can match driven pile economics Krenek Road case: zero end-bearing in dense sand due to clay drilling decompression — CFA should have terminated in clay Retaining walls: secant/tangent, diameters ≤1 m, depths ≤18 m; verticality control critical for watertight walls Pile-supported embankments: ≤15 min/pile cycle time; ~$40/LM for 300–350 mm piles on large projects

figures.caption: Typical Crane-Mounted CFA Rig
figures.description: Construction Equipment Selection of drilling rigs, auger types, and pumping equipment for CFA and DD pile installation Crane-mounted rigs: torque 20–120 kN-m; min 40 kN-m (30,000 ft-lbs) recommended for transportation projects Hydraulic rigs: torque 90–400 kN-m, crowd up to 270 kN; preferred for DD piles requiring high downforce Low headroom rigs: max 28 kN-m, 13 kN crowd; suitable only in most favorable soil conditions Auger pitch must match soil — larger pitch for clay; DD displacement systems are proprietary (DeWaal, Omega, Fundex) Grout pump: positive displacement, max 2.4 MPa (350 psi); volume per stroke ≈ 100 mm of pile length In-line magnetic flowmeter preferred over stroke counter for volume monitoring — stroke count is unreliable

figures.description: Construction Materials Material specifications for grout/concrete and reinforcing steel in CFA piles Grout: more fluid, easier to pump, more susceptible to sulfate/acid attack vs. concrete Target strength: 27.6–34.5 MPa (4,000–5,000 psi); slump 200 ± 25 mm (concrete); flow cone 10–25 sec (grout, modified 19 mm opening) Fly ash retards early strength — mix design must show strength development vs. time; normal strength by 10–14 days Rebar: ASTM A615 Gr. 60; 75 mm min cover; spacers at ≤3 m; cage length typically limited to 10–15 m Steel pipe reinforcement (A572 Gr. 50 or A252 Gr. 2) for high-bending wall/slope stabilization applications Do not place grout/concrete below 4°C (40°F) or above 38°C (100°F) without approved hot/cold weather procedures

shear strength and vertical effective stress in soil CHAPTER 1 INTRODUCTION 1.1 PURPOSE The purpose of this document is to develop a state-of-the-practice manual for the design and construction of continuous flight auger (CFA) piles, including those piles commonly referred to as augered cast-in-place (ACIP) piles, drilled displacement (DD) piles, and screw piles. An Allowable Stress Design (ASD) procedure is presented in this document as resistance (strength reduction) factors have not yet been calibrated for CFA piles for a Load Resistance Factored Design (LRFD) approach. The intended audience for this document is engineers and construction specialists involved in the design, construction, and contracting of foundation elements for transportation structures. 1.2 BACKGROUND CFA piles have been used worldwide and also in the U.S. commercial market, but have not been used frequently for support of transportation structures in the United States. This underutilization of a viable technology is a result of perceived difficulties in quality control and of the difficulties associated with incorporating a rapidly developing (and often proprietary) technology into the traditional, prescriptive design-bid-build concept. Recent advances in automated monitoring and recording devices will alleviate concerns of quality control, as well as provide an essential tool for a performance-based contracting process. A performance-based approach is presented to allow the specialty contractors greater freedom to compete in providing the most cost-effective foundation system while satisfying the project requirements. The performance specification places a greater responsibility for the resulting foundation performance on the contractor or design-build team. Rather than rigorous prescriptive specifications, a comprehensive testing program is used to verify performance. Full-scale load testing is used to verify the load carrying capabilities of the foundations provided. Automatic monitoring and recording devices are used during construction of both test piles and production piles to establish construction parameters (down-force, torque, grout take, etc.), and to verify that these parameters are met for every production pile. Full-scale load testing may be performed on production piles throughout the project, as selected by the owner. This document provides descriptions of CFA pile types, materials, construction equipment, and procedures. Quality control (QC)/quality assurance (QA) procedures are discussed. A performance specification is provided in a format that may be adapted to specific project requirements. Recommendations are made for methods to estimate the static axial capacity of single piles. A thorough evaluation and comparison of various existing methods used in the United States and Europe is presented. Group effects for axial capacity and settlement are discussed, as well as lateral load capacities for both single piles and pile groups. A generalized step-by-step method for the selection and design of CFA piles is presented. 1 1.3 RELEVANT PUBLICATIONS A list of the references used in the development of this manual is presented in Chapter 9. These references include key publications on the design of augered pile foundations. Existing Federal Highway Administration (FWHA) and American Association of State Highway Officials (AASHTO) publications that include engineering principles related to the subject of CFA piles are also included in the references. 1.4 DOCUMENT ORGANIZATION The remainder of this document is organized as follows. • Chapter 2 - Description of Continuous Flight Auger Pile Types and Basic Mechanisms. This chapter provides a general overview of CFA piles, including a description of the main system components, typical equipment, and the sequence of construction. • Chapter 3 - Applications for Transportation Projects. This chapter presents advantages and limitations of CFA piles in transportation projects, describes favorable and unfavorable project and geotechnical conditions, and illustrates applications of CFA piles in transportation projects. • Chapter 4 - Construction Techniques and Materials. This chapter provides details on construction techniques, materials, and recommended practice for the construction of CFA piles in transportation projects. • Chapter 5 - Evaluation of Static Capacity of Continuous Flight Augered Piles. This chapter presents an evaluation and comparison of various existing methods used in the United States and Europe to calculate the static capacity of CFA piles. • Chapter 6 - Recommended Design Method. This chapter presents a step-by-step generalized method for the selection and design of CFA piles. An annotated example is included in this chapter. • Chapter 7 - Quality Control (QC)/Quality Assurance (QA) Procedures. This chapter discusses the use of automated QC/QA equipment and presents guidelines. • Chapter 8 - Guide Construction Specifications for Continuous Flight Auger Piles. This chapter presents a performance specification for CFA piles. • Chapter 9 - References. A list of the references used in this document is presented. • Appendix A - Comparisons of Methods for Estimating the Static Axial Capacity of CFA Piles. • Appendix B - Spreadsheet Solutions for Axial Capacity of Single CFA Piles
